data.title: Colom announces town hall in reddest county of Mississippi
data.description:
Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-Miss.) will hold a town hall next Tuesday in the county where he received the lowest share of the vote in the midterms, he announced earlier this week, aligning with the Democrat’s pledges to be “a senator for all Mississippi.”

“Itawamba County is where I received my lowest percentage of the vote on Election Day. But I promised to be a senator for all Mississippi and I meant it,” Colom wrote in Facebook post Thursday. “No matter where you live or how you voted, your voice matters and I’ll always show up for you.”

Itawamba County is in northeast Mississippi, just east of the city of Tupelo. President Trump carried the county by 80 points in 2024 and received the highest share of the vote in county history for a Republican presidential candidate. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), whom Colom unseated in this year’s Senate race, won Itawamba by nearly 66 points.

The town hall invitation describes the event as “an opportunity to hear directly from Senator-elect Colom, ask questions, and engage in meaningful dialogue.”

Colom defeated Hyde-Smith in a massive upset that took days after the election to call. He is the first Black senator Mississippians have elected by popular vote and the third to ever represent the Magnolia State — the last being Sen. Blanche K. Bruce, who served during the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Although the state of Mississippi is one third Black, according to census data.

The senator-elect made reaching out to Republicans a focal point of his Senate campaign, something he had to do in order to be elected in deep-red Mississippi.

One viral video he posted to social media showed him speaking with voters in line for Trump’s Mississippi rally just days before the election. Colom said in an interview Friday speaking with Trump voters showed him they had a lot in common and were dissatisfied with similar issues.

“I want to represent those people. So, it was my job to go listen to them, and I found out we had a lot in common,” Colom told MS NOW’s Ari Melber. “They were saying the same stuff I was hearing across the state: high gas, high groceries, get out of the war in Iran.”

Even Trump chimed in to Colom’s appearance at his rally, saying in an interview with sports commentator Stephen A. Smith he gave the Democrat “a lot of credit” for campaigning in his line.

data.title: Pelosi reflects on decades-long political career: 'They made me the villain'
data.description:
Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) reflected on her decades-long political journey this week as she gets ready to retire from Congress in 2027.

“They made me the villain,” Pelosi said while discussing how her political career weighed on her family in an interview with “Tea&Vodka” hosted by Ebs Burnough. “You always have to have a villain; they created me as a villain.”

Pelosi also talked about the many difficulties and challenges women face in politics including false narratives, accusations of overspending and portraying women in a “ridiculous” light.

“The impression was that women were more ethical and so what they would want to do is to cut that down right away,” Pelosi said.

She is a two-time House Speaker and the only woman to hold the role in American history. Democrats secured a House majority in the 2006 midterm elections for the first time in more than a decade. Pelosi, who had been the Democratic leader since 2003, became the first female Speaker in U.S. history. 

“Now, we have so many women that it’s a little bit different,” she said, however, “it’s still a challenge for women.”

Earlier this month, Pelosi announced that she would retire from Congress at the end of the term in January 2027. In a video addressing her constituents, she said, “With a grateful heart, I look forward to my final year of service as your proud representative.”

Over the years, Pelosi has had her notable moments.

In 2019, months into her second term as second tenure as Speaker, Pelosi, along with her Democratic colleagues, attended a meeting at the White House with President Trump. The meeting came after House Democrats, led by Pelosi, launched an impeachment inquiry into Trump.

Less than an hour after the meeting started, Pelosi and her colleagues walked out.

In 2020, after Trump’s State of the Union address, Pelosi stood up, ripped pages of the address in half and placed them on the dais. 

During her recent interview, looking back on her career, Pelosi noted, “We really never accomplished what we needed to do … on gun violence,” calling it, “an unfinished business.”

She added that there is a bipartisan community safety bill, but what is needed is background checks, saying, “American people support that but not the Republicans in Congress.”

data.title: The blue wave can fix America's critical food safety and security gaps
data.description:
When millions gather this Thanksgiving, most won’t question the safety of the food on their plates. They’ll assume our government has strict measures in place that protect our food supply from dangerous contaminants that could cause people harm. 

The facts tell a different story. A recent Washington Post investigation found that the Food and Drug Administration has inspected fewer than 8 percent of all major foreign facilities that provide fresh produce to the United States since 2009.  

Think about that: Over 90 percent of the largest international plants that sell fruits and vegetables to America have not received an FDA inspection in nearly two decades. It’s a massive public health blind spot for a country that’s become increasingly reliant on produce imports in recent years. 

The public health threat this poses to Americans isn’t hyperbole. This summer, a multistate outbreak of cyclosporiasis that was linked to iceberg lettuce imported from Mexico sickenednearly 13,000 people, hospitalized over 550 and claimed two lives. The contaminated lettuce came from a Mexican supplier whose operations hadn’t been inspected by the FDA in seven years.  

There have been other contaminations. In September, broccoli sprouts and microgreens imported from New Zealand contaminated with salmonella sickened 34 people across six states. In October, frozen blueberries from Chile were recalled due to an E. coli outbreak that caused 17 illnesses and six hospitalizations.  

In total, the FDA anticipates over 550 food recalls will take place this fiscal cycle, a number consistent with what the agency typically sees in an average year. However, the increasing severity of these events, combined with cutbacks in personnel, has public health experts worried.  

Janet Hamilton of the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists says “the scale and magnitude of outbreaks that we’re facing right now are unprecedented. It’s like we’re being eclipsed by the scale and magnitude of these outbreaks with the staffing levels that we have.”  

She’s right: The very institutions tasked with protecting the U.S. food supply have been weakened by recent federal workforce reductions. Cutbacks at the FDA — over 4,000 people in just the past two years alone — have hampered the government’s ability to prevent recent deadly foodborne contamination events.   

U.S. lawmakers have failed their collective responsibility to ensure the nation’s food regulatory agencies are keeping Americans safe. But a wave of newly elected members to Capitol Hill is expected to bring much needed support for our public health institutions when the next Congress convenes in January.  

Two physicians have been elected to the U.S. Senate. They include pediatrician Annie Andrews in South Carolina and physician and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Both will bring a deep bench of medical and public health experience to federal rulemaking in the nation’s capital.    

They — along with several other incoming members of Congress with science backgrounds — will help ensure facts prevail and lead the way on health policy. They will be important voices who will hold to account the country’s top health official, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., whose initiatives to date have turned the clock back on public health safety. 

These include the removal of 10,000 roles at Health and Human Services, the dismissal of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s vaccine advisory committee and the easing of restrictions on unproven therapies that align with Kennedy’s personal lifestyle choices. A Democratic majority in both chambers of Congress will establish important checks and balances to administration efforts that have put public health at potential risk.  

The advancement of public health food policy will soon be part of the national legislative agenda. Democrats are already pushing support for important food security initiatives, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, whose mission to help low-income families has been decimated under the current Congress.

Public health institutions have endured a steady erosion of trust in America. Restricting federal resources that make it more difficult for them to protect the safety and availability of our food supply will only make it worse. 

Preventing foodborne illness and providing food access for those in need will be a top focus of the next Congress. Whether the Trump administration and Republicans in Congress will work with Democrats to support these important goals to protect the safety of the American people will be up to them. 

Lyndon Haviland, DrPH, MPH, is a distinguished scholar at the CUNY School of Public Health and Health Policy.

data.title: Trump limits Congress's accesses to confidential agency, contractor information
data.description:
President Trump signed an executive order Friday seeking to block Congress from requesting certain information from federal agencies and their employees, an apparent response to Democrats’ threats of sweeping probes into the administration when they take over Congress

The order, titled “Protecting the Executive’s Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting,” says Congress cannot seek information from government workers or contractors without a “valid legislative purpose.”

“The ability of the Congress to seek executive branch information is limited; it cannot seek information from executive branch departments and agencies (agencies), employees, or Federal contractors without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions,” the order reads.

The order also states third-party federal contractors should notify and coordinate with the White House before releasing certain information to Congress.

“All Federal contractors must immediately … notify the White House and the contracting agencies of any pending or future congressional request … and abide by any instructions received from the White House,” the order reads.

If the White House does order administration officials to withhold their communications from a congressional investigation using executive privilege, the dispute could wind up in court. The Justice Department defended the power in a memo issued earlier this year.

Democrats have pledged to investigate Trump and his allies since retaking both congressional majorities in the midterms, striking a similar tone to after the party won the House in the 2018 elections. Incoming House Oversight Committee Chairman Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) sent a message to the administration on election night, posting on social media, “Lawyer up.”

White House Counsel Will Scharf responded with a letter pledging to fight back against Democrats’ probes and also told Democratic ranking members they did not yet have authority to send letters notifying of investigations until they officially hold the majority in January.

Scharf recently issued an internal directive to White House staff saying they must receive the administration’s approval before testifying to Congress.

data.title: With two big wins in court, Trump may leave a lasting mark on defamation law
data.description:
In his final two years in office, President Trump will likely focus on what legacy he will leave in 2029, from the economy to foreign relations to immigration. But one area where he will leave a lasting mark is that of defamation litigation.

Although Trump has been hostile to the core standards of defamation, he has brought an unusually large number of cases as a sitting president and has also lost a costly defamation case (which he just appealed to the Supreme Court for the second time). He has also secured settlements and corrections.

Now, on the eve of ABC reportedly suspending reporters responsible for an alleged hit piece against his family, Trump has landed two significant wins against The New York Times and the BBC in seeking trials over allegedly defamatory statements. Both could set important precedents for future cases if upheld on appeal.

In Florida, U.S. District Judge Steven D. Merryday allowed the majority of counts against The New York Times to go to trial over reporting that suggested Trump had committed criminal acts. The identity of the defendant holds particular significance, since the Times was the media party in the historic decision New York Times v. Sullivan. Indeed, the “actual malice” standard from that case has drawn Trump’s ire in the past.

Over 50 years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that public officials (and later “public figures”) are subject to a higher burden in proving defamation, to allow for greater breathing space for political speech under the First Amendment. Under this standard, an official must show that the publication had actual knowledge of the falsity of its defamatory statement or displayed a reckless disregard as to whether it was true.

In Trump v. New York Times, Trump is suing the Times for $15 billion. The case raises an important question about what constitutes a “reckless disregard” when a newspaper cites “experts” for a statement.

In green-lighting four of the seven original claims, Merryday will require the Times to answer allegations that Susanne Craig and Russ Buettner defamed the President in their article titled “Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father’s Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success.” He noted that the article raised possible complex tax fraud and money laundering allegations without a formal legal opinion or forensic auditing.

Merryday questioned the paper’s reliance on the three cited experts: Lee-Ford Tritt, Associate Dean and Law Professor at the University of Florida; Adam S. Kaufmann, the former chief of investigations for the Manhattan district attorney’s office; and Mitchell Gans, a tax law professor at Hofstra University. Kaufmann declared that the controversy “smells like a crime,” and Tritt that “highly suspicious” actions might constitute criminal tax fraud.

The court rejected the use of experts to meet the burden when they allegedly lacked a solid evidentiary foundation for the article’s factual claims or insinuations. The court chastised the publication of the “superficial characterization” that “someone else has committed a crime of … complex nature” without a “thorough examination of pertinent facts.”

The Times reporters, he added, “know that they don’t know, but they are undeterred.” Thus, the article could constitute “the purposeful avoidance of the truth, a knowing failure that remains actionable, even after Times v. Sullivan.”

Trump also prevailed before Judge Jeffrey Kuntz in Florida in the separate Trump v. BBC case. In that case, he is suing the British media outlet for splicing together two lines from a Trump speech that created a misleading meaning for viewers, suggesting that Trump had incited supporters to riot on Jan. 6, 2021.

The segment involved an act that is anathema to ethical journalists — cutting lines from different parts of a tape and then joining them, as if they were continuous. Even the BBC’s own journalists admitted that what they had done in the segment violated the most basic ethical standards taught in journalism schools.

The case stems from a documentary that aired just a week before the 2024 election, titled “Trump: A Second Chance.” The piece featured this 12-second segment from Trump’s January 6, 2021 speech: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol, and I’ll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell, and if you don’t fight like hell, you’re not going to have a country anymore.”

But those two lines were actually uttered 55 minutes apart from one another. Not only that, but Trump also expressly told his followers to go to the Hill “peacefully” to let their voices be heard.

The BBC, by splicing together those two lines, effectively put an entirely new statement into Trump’s mouth. What was actually said differed significantly from what aired. First, Trump declared: “Now it is up to Congress to confront this egregious assault on our democracy. And after this, we’re going to walk down and I’ll be there with you. We’re going to walk down, we’re going to walk down. Anyone you want but I think right here, we’re going to walk down to the Capitol and we’re going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we’re probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them.”

Fifty-five minutes later, Trump stated: “[B]ut I said ‘Something’s wrong here, Something’s really wrong, can’t have happened.’ And we fight, we fight like hell, and if you don’t fight like hell, you’re not going to have a country anymore.”

Notably, less than a minute later, Trump told his supporters to remain peaceful: “I know that everyone here will soon be marching over to the Capitol building to peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard.”

In this case, Judge Jeffrey Kuntz found that the BBC recognized its violation of journalistic ethics but still actively sought to guarantee that the misleading segment would be heard before the election.

And the court also found sufficient evidence of actual malice to proceed. “Editing is often required,” Kuntz wrote. “However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech. BBC also had the entire speech available to them for nearly three years by the time of the documentary.”

Once again, it is very difficult for public officials and public figures to prevail under the “actual malice” standard. But although Trump has lost other cases against such outlets as the Wall Street Journal and CNN, these cases represent substantial wins. I previously wrote that Trump was mistaken in calling for a legislative change to the New York Times v. Sullivan standard, which is constitutionally based and not subject to legislative change. But he may now be close to achieving a meaningful clarification of the underlying standards governing the media.

If these rulings are upheld — and especially if he wins either case on the merits — he could win, in his own words, “bigly” in the area of defamation.

Jonathan Turley is the best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.” He teaches torts and defamation. Turley previously worked as BBC’s legal analyst.

data.title: Cotton claims Lutnick ignored his 'many letters' warning of chip sales to China
data.description:
Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored his warnings about U.S. AI chips being smuggled into China, long before reports surfaced about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“If Howard Lutnick wanted my support, perhaps he should have responded to my many letters warning about these Chinese communist front companies and, more importantly, taking the threats of communist China more seriously,” Cotton said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal published Friday.

Cotton, who recently won his reelection campaign in Arkansas and chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Journal Lutnick and his deputies ignored correspondence for over a year about companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips, including Singapore-based company Megaspeed — at the center of Huang’s high-profile departure from the company.

The GOP senator said he sent a letter to Lutnick calling for an investigation into Megaspeed in October 2025.

Alice Huang, a former executive and major shareholder at Megaspeed, was accused of illegally smuggled AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with the former Nvidia CEO.

The tech giant’s chief resigned on Nov. 12 as these reports garnered national attention. The resignation came a day after The New York Times reported Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.

The incident has sparked questions and calls for transparency on both sides of the aisle.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats, Reps. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (Calif.) and Gregory Meeks (N.Y.), are pressing Lutnick for information about the Commerce Department’s investigation into Megaspeed.

“The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter to Lutnick Thursday.

On the Republican side, Rep. Brett Guthrie (Ky.), chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, requested earlier this week that interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress and Lutnick appear before the panel to answer questions.

data.title: House to consider modified version of Protect College Sports Act
data.description:
The House will consider a slightly modified version of the Protect College Sports Act, a landmark bill governing college sports, as Congress aims to pass it into law before the end of the year.

The bill already passed the Senate in a sweeping bipartisan vote in late September.

After months of chaos surrounding player eligibility, the transfer portal, name, image and likeness (NIL) money and a slew of lawsuits, a bipartisan group of lawmakers have stressed the need to pass the bill as soon as possible. 

The act would give the NCAA the authority to enforce its own rules and shield it from lawsuits, one of the single biggest changes aimed at resolving a patchwork of rulings around the country that have left player eligibility uncertain and different across different jurisdictions.

The House’s latest tweak raises the cap on teams permitted in a conference from 20 to 22, opening the door to further conference realignment and expansion.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), one of the bill’s co-sponsors and biggest supporters, along with Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), stressed the need for change in a Senate floor speech advocating for the bill.

“Now I know some argue that college sports are doing just fine. They point to high television ratings, enthusiastic fan bases, and packed stadiums,” Cruz said. ”But popularity does not demonstrate that the system is healthy. It simply proves that the system is worth saving.”

The bill is backed by President Trump and GOP House leadership, but the clock is ticking on final passage — given some Democrats’ concerns about the bill, it may need to pass before the end of the year, after which Democrats will take a sizable majority in both chambers of Congress.

Trump praised the Senate’s passage of the bill back in September, calling it a “really big deal.”

“It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Also supporting the bill is the NCAA and many of the top conferences, including the Big 10 and Southeastern conferences.

data.title: Live updates: House races uncalled nearly 3 weeks post-election; Congress recesses
data.description:
Lawmakers are leaving Capitol Hill on Saturday after a jam-packed week of moving bills and confirming appointments, with the 119th Congress seeking to see through its legislative priorities before it permanently adjourns in January.

Leaders on both sides of the aisle, including Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), expressed frustration this week with Congress members’ low attendance in the lame duck session — especially with bills on permitting reform and Iran war powers reached the floor. Johnson urged his GOP colleagues to “show up and vote” for their remaining days in office.

Meanwhile, Democrats are still waiting to see what their final tally will be in the lower chamber, especially after this week’s leadership elections. Some House races are still undecided almost three weeks after Election Day, many of which have the potential to bolster the Democratic majority. Insiders can read more from The Hill’s Julia Mueller on the outstanding contests here.

President Trump will remain in Washington, D.C., this weekend following his high-stakes trip to Asia, during which he engaged in a rare trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Trump held a 90-minute press briefing Friday afternoon to discuss the visit, though the conference quickly pivoted to other topics — including recent tech outages, the latest on Iran’s reported “dirty bomb” threat and how he will work with Democrats in January.

Follow live below.

data.title: License plate scanners defy the Constitution — courts must uphold drivers' privacy rights
data.description:
A federal court in northern Oklahoma has set an important example for how courts should address Fourth Amendment challenges to automatic license plate readers.

Just last month, in United States v. Kyle, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma granted a motion to suppress evidence collected via automatic license plate readers. Based on nothing more than an out-of-state plate, a Tulsa County deputy sheriff entered Melisa Kyle’s license plate number into a system database and, with a single search, obtained a month’s worth of her location history across multiple states — all without a warrant.

Kyle argued that the warrantless search of her location history violated her Fourth Amendment rights. The court agreed.

This decision marks the first time a federal court has held that the government’s warrantless collection and use of historical license plate location data violates the Constitution. Other courts confronting these increasingly pervasive surveillance systems should follow its lead.

In U.S. v. Knotts (1983), the Supreme Court ruled that a person “traveling in an automobile on public thoroughfares has no reasonable expectation of privacy in his movements.” This ruling has become a favorite precedent invoked by proponents of automatic license plate readers since, they argue, the readers capture only public movements. But that reasoning does not hold up when comparing the technologies involved in these cases. 

In Knotts, police used a primitive radio transmitter to follow a suspect’s vehicle on a single journey. The device merely supplemented the officers’ own surveillance. Today’s automatic readers are a different beast entirely. These systems routinely photograph passing vehicles, record their locations, and store that information in searchable databases. With a few keystrokes, law enforcement can piece together weeks or months of a person’s movements, without any suspicion of wrongdoing.

The distinction is not merely one of technological sophistication, but of the sheer scale, ease and intrusiveness of the surveillance.

Other major decisions in recent years have recognized the importance of considering technological advances when determining how the Fourth Amendment constrains the government in its use of surveillance technologies. 

Less than a decade ago, in Carpenter v. United States, the Supreme Court stated that “a person does not surrender all Fourth Amendment protection by venturing into the public sphere.” The court held there that individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy “in the whole of their physical movements.”

In Carpenter, the court recognized that the government’s use of cell-site location information to track a person’s movements over an extended period can violate this reasonable expectation of privacy. Even when those movements occur publicly, an extensive record can reveal intimate details about a person’s life. 

In June, the Supreme Court built on Carpenter’s principles in Chatrie v. U.S., holding that the government’s acquisition of cellphone location history constitutes a Fourth Amendment search regardless of the amount of data collected. The court considered as critical factors the surveillance’s retrospective nature, its potential for indiscriminate use, its low cost and ease of deployment, and its ability to reveal sensitive information through both short- and long-term tracking. 

The Kyle ruling applied these same principles to automatic license plate readers, which similarly allow the government to systematically collect and retrospectively search location histories. Like cellphone location data, these records can reveal far more about a person’s life than any individual observation on a public road.

Perhaps most troubling is that the automatic reader system allows the collection of vast amounts of location data about ordinary Americans who are not suspected of any wrongdoing, and who often do not even realize they are being tracked in the first place. Rather than identifying a suspect and then conducting surveillance, these systems allow police to collect data indiscriminately and look for evidence of wrongdoing later. The ease and efficiency of this technology make it all the more important that courts impose meaningful constitutional limits on its use.

The Fourth Amendment was not written with automatic license plate readers in mind, but its protections were never meant to become obsolete as technology evolves. By recognizing the constitutional implications of prolonged, warrantless location tracking, Kyle offers an approach that accounts for the realities of modern surveillance. 

Other courts confronting these systems should recognize the distinction between observing a car on a public road and giving the government the ability to reconstruct a person’s movements over weeks or months. Technological advances may have transformed the government’s surveillance capabilities, but they have not diminished Americans’ Fourth Amendment rights.

Andreia Trifoi is litigation counsel at the New Civil Liberties Alliance.

data.title: California State Bar places Katie Zacharia under investigation
data.description:
The California State Bar Association is investigating former White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia, a newly-released letter shows, after a watchdog group filed a complaint accusing her of violating the law.

Zacharia served a brief five-day stint as press secretary, but during that period, reporting emerged that she had never passed the bar exam despite claiming to be an attorney.

Nonprofit watchdog group Campaign for Accountability (CfA) wrote a letter to the state bar on Oct. 14, saying Zacharia had broken California law, asking the bar association to open an investigation.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie,” CfA executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a release about the group’s letter. “The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has.”

The state bar responded Nov. 6 in a letter recently made public, confirming it had opened an investigation.

California law prohibits anyone who is not licensed by the state bar from presenting themselves as a lawyer, and a conviction is a misdemeanor “punishable by up to one year in a county jail or by a fine of up to one thousand dollars ($1,000), or by both that fine and imprisonment.”

A spokesperson for Zacharia called the allegations “baseless” and “politically motivated” in a statement to the Los Angeles Times.

Zacharia was announced as White House press secretary a few weeks after the departure of Karoline Leavitt, who had served in the role since President Trump returned to office. The president promoted Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her for the role, though that was not a requirement for the role.

The complaint from the CfA specifically outlines times when she claimed to be an attorney, including several on-air appearances as a legal analyst.

“She has been identified on screen as a lawyer in at least 18 Fox News appearances since March 2025, has claimed to have served as ‘outside counsel’ to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation, and listed herself as full-time General Counsel of Fix California, a California-based nonprofit, from January 2024 to March 2025,” the CfA said in its release about the complaint.

After completing one short press briefing, reporting emerged that she was not on record in any state for passing the bar, and Trump announced her departure after just a few days on the job.

Kuppersmith praised the state bar’s decision to launch an investigation.

“Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” she said in a Thursday release. “We’re pleased the California Bar is taking this matter seriously and investigating.”
